story.name: ジャスミンの きっさてん
story.title: Regulars
story.line: マスターが はじめて おきゃくさんに なります
story.ja: 数週間たち、リトル・ケトルには常連ができた。毎朝同じものを頼むちゃちゃまる、窓ぎわで本を読むキャラメル、クロスワードをするたぬきち。ある休みの日、ついにマスターが客として来る。緊張しながらいれたコーヒーに、マスターはひとこと「うん。いいコーヒーだ」。そして、常連の名前をおぼえていることこそが仕事だと言う。閉店後、カップを洗い、灯りを消して、島は静かに眠る。

segments.en: A few weeks went by, the way weeks do on an island. The days got shorter, the mornings got colder, and The Little Kettle got a little busier.
Pekoe started to learn the rhythm of the place.
Who came early, who came late, who wanted to talk, and who just wanted to be left alone with a cup.
Dom came every morning at seven fifteen, right after his run. Every morning, he ordered an iced latte, even though it was almost winter.
The usual, please! I know, I know, it's cold out. But I'm, like, super warm from running. It works, trust me.
Goldie came on Tuesdays and Thursdays and sat in her spot by the window. She read mystery novels and always guessed the ending, and always acted surprised anyway.
Tom Nook came every afternoon at three for a drip coffee and the crossword puzzle. He did it in pen.
He never asked for help, but sometimes he read a clue out loud, just in case.
Five letters, a coffee drink with lots of milk. Hmm. Yes, yes, I believe I've got it. Thank you, Pekoe.
She learned that Mabel liked her latte extra hot, and that the fishermen liked their coffee black and their honey toast extra crispy.
She learned everyone's name, and how they took their coffee, and what kind of day they were having, just from the way they opened the door.
And then one quiet Wednesday morning, the door opened very slowly, and Brewster came in.
Not to fix anything. Not to drop anything off. He came in and sat down.
Pekoe almost dropped the cup she was holding. Dom stopped talking in the middle of a sentence. Even Goldie looked up from her book.
It's my day off. One drip coffee, please. No rush.
Pekoe's paws were shaking a little as she measured the beans. His beans, the ones from the paper bag.
She did it slowly and carefully, the way he had taught her without ever really teaching her.
She poured the hot water in slow circles and waited. Brewster watched every step without a word. The whole café was so quiet, you could hear the kettle.
She set the cup down in front of him. He picked it up. He smelled it.
He took one small sip. And then he put the cup down and looked at it for a very long time.
Hm. Good. That's good coffee, Pekoe.
That was all. A handful of words, which, from Brewster, is practically a speech.
But Dom cheered so loudly that a seagull outside flew off the railing, and Goldie had to wipe her eyes with a napkin.
Thank you. Really. I couldn't have done any of this without you. The machine, the beans, the advice, all of it.
You did the hard part yourself. You know everyone's name. You know how they like their coffee. That's the whole job.
He finished his coffee, left a coin on the counter, and nodded to her on his way out.
And the next Wednesday, he came back. And the one after that.
That night, after the last customer had gone home, Pekoe stayed late to close up, the way she did every night now.
She washed the cups, one by one, and set them upside down to dry. She wiped the long wooden counter until it shone in the lamplight.
She read the napkin on the wall, and the note next to it.
She straightened the sign that said The Litle Kettle, and smiled at the missing T, like always.
Then she turned off the lamps, one by one, until only the little light over the door was left. She stepped out and locked up.
Outside, the island was asleep. The water was calm. A few windows were still glowing up the hill, and somewhere, somebody's kettle was starting to whistle.
Pekoe walked home slowly, with her hands in her pockets and the smell of coffee still in her fur. Tomorrow, the usual. Goodnight.
